evidence_notes.finding: A multi-vocal review of 114 academic and grey-literature sources finds that reliability, security, cost and verification problems in LLM multi-agent code generation are systemic architectural weaknesses rather than isolated model failures, and that current benchmarks provide insufficient evaluation of multi-agent collaboration and coordination. The authors conclude the field is shifting from a model-centric phase to a systems-engineering phase where coordination stability, verification pipelines and cost governance dominate.
evidence_notes.quote: Existing benchmarks often have limited real-world representativeness, lack scalability to large or long-horizon tasks, involve high computational costs, and provide insufficient evaluation of multi-agent collaboration and coordination.

extraction.benchmark: 14 benchmarks identified across 52 of 114 studies; HumanEval most frequent (29 uses), plus MBPP, SWE-bench (6), SWE-bench Lite (4), APPS, EvalPlus
extraction.key_results: 114 studies reviewed. Nine motivation categories for adopting multi-agent systems, led by performance enhancement (12/114, 10.5%) and complex task handling (9/114, 7.9%). Challenges synthesized into 6 categories and 26 subcategories: computational and resource constraints (15/114, 13.2%; computational cost 7.9%, communication overhead 3.5%), security and privacy risk (11/114, 9.7%), context and memory limitations (11/114, 9.7%). Closed-source GPT models dominate. Authors conclude current agent systems are largely prototype-level and lack the reliability and scalability needed for production deployment.
extraction.limitations: Multi-vocal design mixes peer-reviewed and grey literature of uneven rigor; findings are synthesized from self-reported claims rather than independent replication; the review notes that reported benchmark performance may not translate to real-world software development, and that no controlled comparison of multi-agent versus single-agent configurations is performed by the review itself.

evidence_notes.finding: In smart-contract auditing, a decentralized multi-agent design outperformed a centralized scheduler that implemented identical risk-aware planning and repair logic (F1 0.87 vs 0.83), with the advantage concentrated under injected failures rather than under normal conditions, at a measured coordination overhead of 4.2%.
evidence_notes.quote: SPEAR achieves higher overall effectiveness than all baselines, including a centralized scheduler that implements identical planning and repair logic.

extraction.framework: SPEAR (Strategic Planning, Execution, and Automated Repair)
extraction.agent_count: 5 specialized agents (Planning, Execution, Repair, Safe Actuation, Coordination)
extraction.benchmark: Damn Vulnerable DeFi (15 challenges, 10 runs per configuration); 500 security objectives from GitHub Solidity contracts; one DeFi protocol (47 contracts, 12 vulnerabilities)
extraction.baseline: Centralized Scheduler with identical planning/repair logic; Sequential Pipeline (Slither -> Mythril -> Echidna); Slither only; Slither + Mythril; plus ablations (No Protocols, No Autonomy, No Self-Healing, Rigid Pipeline)
extraction.key_results: SPEAR F1 0.87 (P 0.89 / R 0.85) vs Centralized Scheduler 0.83, Sequential Pipeline 0.82, Slither+Mythril 0.78, Slither only 0.73. Ablations over 20 audit sessions with injected failures: protocols give 1.8x faster recovery (2.3 vs 4.1 min, p<0.01) and 15% fewer LLM invocations; autonomy 2.1x faster (2.3 vs 4.8 min); self-healing 3.2x faster (2.3 vs 7.4 min, p<0.001) and 31% fewer LLM invocations; Rigid Pipeline recovery 8.7 min. Coordination overhead 4.2% (std 1.1%), mean 47 messages per audit, O(|A|) message scaling. PFIR test repair 94% success with 64% deterministic fixes. Planning agent cut Time to First Critical Vulnerability from 54 to 18 minutes. Average cost $2.30 per audit (Claude Sonnet 4.5).
extraction.limitations: Controlled failure injection may not capture all real-world failure modes; ablation comparisons assume implementations are equivalent apart from the ablated component; evaluation uses a synthetic DVD benchmark plus one DeFi protocol, with modest sample sizes (15 challenges, 20 audit sessions); the tool-completeness assumption underlying the liveness proof is strong so liveness is probabilistic in practice; F1 and TFCV may not capture report clarity or false-positive cost; PFIR success measures compilation/execution rather than semantic test correctness; the Coordinator Agent is a potential single point of failure.

evidence_notes.finding: Surveying 139 papers across six SE topics, the authors argue LLM-based agents extend single LLMs through role specialization, iterative refinement and tool integration, but that multi-agent workflow complexity introduces synchronization, state-consistency and cascading-misunderstanding problems that single LLM pipelines do not exhibit, with no unified agent definition or evaluation protocol available.
evidence_notes.quote: Traditional LLMs excel at isolated tasks but face limitations due to constrained context awareness, insufficient feedback mechanisms, and minimal autonomy.

extraction.benchmark: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-ET, HumanEval-X, CodeSearchNet, Spider, BIRD, ToolBench, APIBench, CAASD
extraction.baseline: LLMs (single-model prompting/fine-tuning) compared against LLM-based agents across six SE topics
extraction.key_results: 139 papers reviewed across requirement engineering, code generation, autonomous decision-making, software design, test generation, and maintenance. Single-model approaches can reach high pass@k on established benchmarks, but agent-based systems show broader coverage of large-scale, multi-file tasks. Six named challenges: (1) no standardized agent definition or evaluation protocol; (2) workflow complexity and error propagation in multi-agent systems, where asynchronous interaction is more prone to cascading misunderstandings and state/semantic alignment remains open; (3) fragile tool integration; (4) weak cross-task generalization; (5) scarcity of interactive multi-turn simulation datasets; (6) cognitive transparency and trust. Agent-specific metrics (Win Rate, Agreement Rate, Execution Effectiveness, Cost Efficiency) supplement Pass@k.
extraction.limitations: Narrative survey without a formal systematic-review protocol or quality appraisal; the boundary between an LLM and an LLM-based agent is acknowledged to be unsettled, so classification of the reviewed work is partly judgmental; performance comparisons are drawn from heterogeneous primary studies rather than controlled experiments; benchmark coverage is skewed toward static input-output tasks that the authors say cannot evaluate negotiation, role conflict resolution, or tool-driven reasoning.

evidence_notes.finding: On five non-trivial tasks in a ~180K-line Next.js repository, a context-engineered hub-and-spoke multi-agent Claude Code system succeeded on 4/5 tasks (80%) without human correction versus 2/5 (40%) for a single-agent Claude baseline, at roughly 3-5x the token cost; the baseline's failures were dominated by missed cross-file edits and hallucinated APIs.
evidence_notes.quote: Out of 5 tasks attempted (including feature additions and bug fixes of varying complexity), our system achieved a successful outcome (defined by passing all tests and meeting the acceptance criteria) on 4 tasks (80%) without any human corrections.

extraction.framework: Context-engineering pipeline: GPT-5 Intent Translator + Elicit semantic retrieval + NotebookLM synthesis + Claude Code multi-agent system with vector DB (ChromaDB/Zilliz) and MCP tools
extraction.agent_count: 1 orchestrator plus 4+ specialist sub-agents (backend-architect, frontend-specialist, devops-engineer, code-reviewer; a database-migrator agent was added ad hoc)
extraction.baseline: single-agent Claude Code with only a CLAUDE.md context file and direct user prompts
extraction.key_results: 4/5 tasks (80%) succeeded first-pass without human correction vs 2/5 (40%) for the single-agent baseline. Multi-agent runs exchanged ~30-40 messages and ~100k tokens per task versus 10k-20k for the baseline (about 3-5x more tokens on successful tasks), though the baseline's retry and debugging chats pushed it toward ~50k on complex tasks. Semantic code retrieval eliminated hallucinated API calls (e.g., the baseline invented refreshToken() while the multi-agent system used the real renewSession()). Isolated per-agent context windows plus a five-layer context stack (task spec, external knowledge, project memory, retrieved code, execution artifacts) are credited with the gains; a dedicated reviewer agent caught null-pointer and security issues the coding agents missed.
extraction.limitations: Only five tasks on a single proprietary codebase, evaluated qualitatively with no statistical testing and no independent replication; dependence on external retrieval quality caused at least one case where an irrelevant Elicit paper added noise and confused the Planner; the orchestrator follows a fixed plan-code-test-review sequence and cannot dynamically re-plan; early runs saw two agents editing the same file and steps dropped between agents, mitigated only by prompt refinement and a file lock; results rely on a comprehensive existing test suite, so sparse tests could cause false completion; error tracing across agents requires manual log analysis; computational cost may not scale.

evidence_notes.finding: Extraction not possible: the retrieved text file does not contain this article. It contains a different paper from the same journal issue (DOI 10.22266/ijies2025.1231.01, 'A GAN-based Digital Image Watermarking Model with Attention Augmented Feature Extractor and Spatial Transformer'). The file contains zero occurrences of 'agent', 'incident', 'root cause', or 'Site Reliability'.

extraction.limitations: Wrong article retrieved; re-fetch required for DOI 10.22266/ijies2025.1231.28.

evidence_notes.finding: In a controlled 270-execution comparison on TestEval unit-test generation with one model held constant, the Sequential pipeline beat the Single-Agent baseline (92.2% vs 81.1% success) while the Hierarchical supervisor-worker pattern underperformed the single agent badly (54.4% success, 28.54% test failure rate, 3.7x the cost); every hierarchical failure was attributed to a 'supervisor information bottleneck' in which the supervisor never relayed the analyst's reasoning to the writer.
evidence_notes.quote: The Sequential pattern recorded the highest success rate (92.2%), the lowest latency variance (295.56 s2), and a competitive cost (0.089 USD per task).

extraction.framework: Custom implementations of three coordination patterns (Single-Agent Baseline, Sequential, Hierarchical) on Claude Sonnet 4; preceded by a structured review of 31 articles yielding a taxonomy of 10 coordination patterns
extraction.agent_count: 1 (single-agent), a sequential chain, and a supervisor plus 2 workers (analyst, writer) for the hierarchical pattern
extraction.key_results: 30 tasks x 3 runs x 3 architectures = 270 executions, Claude Sonnet 4, temperature 0.2. Success: Sequential 92.2% (87/90), Single-Agent 81.1%, Hierarchical 54.4% (49/90, 47% cross-run variability). Line/branch coverage: 91.6%/90.6% Sequential, 80.6%/79.7% Single-Agent, ~54% Hierarchical. Test failure rate: 1.41% Sequential, 2.83% Single-Agent, 28.54% Hierarchical. Cost per task: 0.083 USD Single-Agent, 0.089 USD Sequential, 0.308 USD Hierarchical. Hierarchical had the highest median latency (142.37 s); Single-Agent was the least consistent on resource metrics (latency CV 60.6%, input-token CV 71.0%). Error counts show delegation_leak (11) and syntax_error (12) unique to or concentrated in Hierarchical. Across all 41 hierarchical failures no direct worker-to-worker information flow was observed; the supervisor re-delegated to the analyst instead of forwarding the analyst's rationale to the writer.
extraction.limitations: Single LLM (Claude Sonnet 4), single benchmark family (TestEval), and a single SE task type (unit test generation); only three runs per architecture, which the authors say may not capture LLM output variability; no per-architecture prompt optimization, so gaps may reflect prompt sensitivity rather than architecture; TestEval is built on public LeetCode problems, raising benchmark contamination and memorization concerns that could shift the absolute pass rates; qualitative coding was done by a single researcher with no inter-rater agreement, and the Coordination overhead category had to be dropped for lack of independent evidence; test failure rate measures internal consistency rather than true error recovery.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 12 Designer:Programmer agent pairs from 7 open-source LLMs on a single C programming task, convergence, role alignment and compilation success were not correlated: only DeepSeek-R1:DeepSeek-R1 converged and sustained a correct solution, several pairs achieved 100% compilation while never reaching a correct solution, and pairs that diverged after 3, 21 or 69 iterations never recovered.
evidence_notes.quote: This suggests that once a correct solution emerges, it tends to be preserved for a bounded number of iterations (≤ 69 in our study), while later recovery is unlikely.

extraction.framework: Lightweight custom Python controller enforcing deterministic turn-taking between a Designer agent and a Programmer agent (models served via Ollama 0.12.10)
extraction.key_results: 12 Designer:Programmer pairs from Gemma 2, Gemma 3, LLaMA 3.2, LLaMA 3.3, DeepSeek-R1, MiniCPM and Qwen3; temperature 0.5, max 4096 tokens, iteration cap 10,000, each pair run twice. Three success/failure patterns identified: SFP1 successful convergence, SFP2 non-initiating, SFP3 divergence. Only DeepSeek-R1:DeepSeek-R1 converged from the first iteration and sustained it, yet had only 3.29% compilation success and 68-95% 'No Code Found' turns. LLaMA3.2:LLaMA3.2 and Qwen3:Qwen3 reached 100% compilation success with strong role alignment but never started from the correct solution (Qwen3 37% semantic echoing). DeepSeek-R1:MiniCPM and LLaMA3.3:LLaMA3.3 dropped to 30-40% success with up to 62% failures. Divergent pairs (Qwen3:DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1:LLaMA3.3, LLaMA3.3:LLaMA3.3) had produced the correct solution in iteration 1 and diverged after 3, 21 and 69 iterations respectively, with no observed recovery. Reasoning models paired with non-reasoning models produced semantic echoing without task progression. Inter-rater agreement Cohen's kappa = 0.71.
extraction.limitations: BLEU and ROUGE may not capture non-literal correctness or paraphrased reasoning, mitigated only by manual annotation; a single open-ended Fibonacci game task means correctness and convergence judgments are sensitive to the chosen evaluation criteria and results may not generalize across tasks, prompts or programming languages; limited to 12 open-source LLM combinations with fixed minimal prompts and fixed role conditioning, so findings may not transfer to proprietary models, longer dialogues or dynamic role shifts; repeated runs are not reported separately.

evidence_notes.finding: Connecting 50+ benchmarks to prompt-based, fine-tuning-based and agent-based solution paradigms across 150+ papers, the survey argues that existing multi-agent SE frameworks rely on simplistic coordination (sequential pipelines or centralized orchestration) that cannot express real development workflows, and that no benchmarks measure coordination efficiency or communication overhead.
evidence_notes.quote: Current multi-agent frameworks often rely on simple coordination mechanisms such as sequential pipelines or centralized orchestration, which fail to capture the dynamic, iterative, and often non-linear nature of real software development workflows.

extraction.benchmark: 50+ benchmarks catalogued and mapped to solution strategies, spanning code generation, translation and repair (e.g. SWE-bench, HumanEval)
extraction.baseline: Taxonomic comparison of prompt-based vs fine-tuning-based vs agent-based paradigms
extraction.key_results: 150+ papers reviewed. Multi-agent role decomposition is the dominant agentic pattern, exemplified by MAGIS (Manager/Developer/QA Engineer), AgileCoder (Product Manager/Tester), MASAI (Test Template Generator, Issue Reproducer, Edit Localizer, Fixer, Ranker), Co-PatcheR (localization/generation/validation), XpandA (Explorer agents) and staged planners (Codes, LLMDFA, DRCodePilot, MarsCode). Identified coordination challenges: communication protocols between differently specialized agents, redundant or conflicting edits to the same codebase, dependency and precedence management, and resource allocation across the collective. Proposed directions include decentralized coordination protocols, shared memory architectures with consistent codebase views, conflict-resolution and distributed-consensus algorithms, temporal-logic verification of coordination protocols, complementary role pairing (creative generator with rigorous verifier; bottom-up implementer with top-down architect), plus new benchmarks measuring coordination efficiency and communication overhead. Also flags an accountability vacuum around IP attribution, liability, unsustainable compute scaling, developer deskilling, and the need for verifiable audit trails and provenance tracking.
extraction.limitations: Descriptive taxonomy without controlled experiments or quantitative meta-analysis; benchmark-to-solution mappings are derived from primary-study self-reports rather than re-execution; the survey explicitly notes that agents degrade on domain-specific languages, legacy codebases and specialized domains because training data is imbalanced, and that current evaluation does not measure coordination efficiency, communication overhead or graceful handling of dynamic requirements.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 8 pipeline configurations of 3 frontier LLMs on 3 benchmarks, an unstructured Planner-Executor-Critic pipeline fell below a competent monolithic model, while adding a structured accountable handoff raised accuracy by up to 36.22 points; blame attribution showed the Planner dominates failure (error rate 7.35% for the best model vs 40.49% for the worst) at a cost of 2-3x spend and 8-10x latency.
evidence_notes.quote: Without clear roles and checks, errors compound across stages and accuracy falls below a competent single model.

extraction.framework: Traceable/accountable sequential pipeline with blame attribution (Planner -> Executor -> Critic), instrumented for stagewise repair/harm/no-op flags and error-origin assignment
extraction.benchmark: PythonIO (127 prompts), LogiQA (283 prompts), AGIEval (263 prompts)
extraction.baseline: Monolithic single-model end-to-end answering, plus Simple (non-accountable) pipelines of the same configurations
extraction.key_results: 8 ordered triples of GPT-4o (A), Claude Sonnet 4 (B) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (C). Accountable vs Simple pipeline accuracy deltas: PythonIO BBB +36.22 (61.42% -> 97.64%), BAB +33.07, CBA +27.56, CCA +26.78; AgiEval AAA +19.78 (57.41% -> 77.19%), ABC +9.50; LogiQA gains modest (CCA +3.76 to +6.99). A few configurations regressed slightly (AgiEval BAB -2.28, BCC -0.76; PythonIO BCC -0.78). Planner error rates: Gemini 7.35% (AgiEval) / 0.79% (PythonIO) / 15.19% (LogiQA); Claude 13.43/3.94/22.03; GPT-4o 40.49/11.02/28.62. Role behaviours: Claude best Executor (repair 10.01%, harm 0.25%); GPT-4o highest Critic repair (5.20%) but highest Executor harm (1.33%); Claude highest Critic harm (1.90%); Gemini lowest harm (0.25%) in both roles. Recommended casting: Gemini Planner -> Claude Executor -> GPT-4o Critic. Heterogeneous pipelines (CBA, CCA) frequently sit on the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier. Accountability cost ~2-3x spend and median latency from ~2s to 20-25s (roughly 8-10x slower).
extraction.limitations: Construct validity: all three benchmarks are multiple-choice, which makes blame attribution tractable but may not reflect open-ended real-world software engineering. Internal validity: blame assignment presumes ground-truth labels that are unavailable at runtime, so deployments would need proxies such as self-consistency checks, verifier agents or unit tests. External validity: results come from three proprietary LLMs inside a fixed evaluation window and may shift with model updates; extension to open-source models is left to future work.

evidence_notes.finding: Surveying 55 papers on LLM agent trajectory analysis, the authors show automated failure attribution remains weak: step-level attribution accuracy on the Who&When benchmark spans only about 25-52%, with agent-level accuracy substantially higher, and benchmark diversity is the field's bottleneck. Multi-agent failure taxonomies (MAST) attribute failures to specification issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.
evidence_notes.quote: In terms of reported accuracy, on the Who&When benchmark, reported step-level attribution accuracy varies substantially across techniques, ranging from about 25% [11] to 52% [39].

extraction.baseline: Comparison of attribution paradigms (LLM prompting, causal inference, fine-tuned tracer models, dynamic intervention) against each other on Who&When
extraction.key_results: 55 papers (early 2025 to April 2026) organized along failure taxonomy, failure attribution, system enhancement, monitoring tools, and datasets/benchmarks. Four taxonomic perspectives, four attribution paradigms, three enhancement families. MAST identifies 14 failure modes in 3 categories: specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification (including premature termination). Most prevalent failure families across taxonomies: instruction and format fidelity; task planning and decomposition; interaction, state and coordination (step repetition and reasoning-action mismatch prevalent in multi-agent settings); knowledge and reasoning limits. Step-level attribution accuracy on Who&When ranges ~25% to 52%; TraceElephant currently ~33%. Agent-level accuracy is consistently higher than step-level; algorithm-generated systems are easier to attribute than hand-crafted ones; fine-tuning-based methods perform relatively best. Benchmarks are shifting toward full observability and unrecoverable-failure annotation.
extraction.limitations: The survey states comparability across attribution studies remains limited due to differences in datasets, observability settings and evaluation protocols; Who&When is almost the only benchmark built specifically for failure attribution, so benchmark diversity is a bottleneck; reported step-level accuracy is acknowledged as still limited; agent-level or step-level accuracy may not reflect real diagnostic utility.

evidence_notes.finding: With three agent architectures implemented on a unified toolset to remove engineering confounds, a Dev-Test multi-agent workflow beat a single agent (49.48% vs 45.72% requirement implementation rate) while a Design-Dev-Test workflow collapsed to 27.71%, showing multi-agent decomposition helps only when well structured; 55.8% of all failures originated in planning (requirement omission 27.9%, misinterpretation 22.2%) rather than code implementation.
evidence_notes.quote: The results in Table 5, clearly indicate that “Task Planning” is the primary bottleneck in current agent systems, accounting for 55.8% of all issues.

extraction.framework: SDAgent, implemented in three variants on a unified engineering standard and toolset: SDAgent-Single, SDAgent-DT (Dev + Test agents), SDAgent-DDT (Design + Dev + Test agents)
extraction.benchmark: E2EDevBench (dynamically curated from recent PyPI projects), evaluated with a hybrid framework combining migrated test cases and fine-grained LLM-as-Judge requirement verification
extraction.baseline: SDAgent-Single (single-agent workflow) on the identical toolset
extraction.key_results: Requirement implementation rate: SDAgent-DT 49.48% > SDAgent-Single 45.72% > SDAgent-DDT 27.71% (state-of-the-art agents fulfil roughly 50% of requirements). SDAgent-DT + Gemini-2.5-Pro consumed 5.24M tokens sent and 49.65K generated per project at about $7.05. Weaker Flash sometimes beat Pro (48.46% vs 42.97% in the single-agent setting) by spending 4x the tokens (20.90M vs 4.96M) on trial and error, while Pro appears prone to premature self-submission. SDAgent-Single writes tests early (first test at step 11.56 vs 27.96 for DT), which the authors argue causes reactive local-fixing loops and 'subtask immersion' that abandons the global plan. SDAgent-DDT underperforms because the Design Agent's authoritative plan is followed over the original requirements, propagating design flaws downstream. Failure taxonomy: incorrect implementation 34.1%, missing component/feature 32.4%, incomplete implementation 18.1%, dependent/upstream cascading failure 15.3%. Root causes: Task Planning 55.8% (omission 27.9%, misinterpretation 22.2%, architectural design flaw 5.6%), Task Execution 38.6% (dependent feature failure 21.0%, superficial implementation 12.5%, technical bottleneck 3.2%, context/task forgetting 1.9%), Task Verification 5.7%. Performance was stable on unseen 2025-Q1 data (42% vs 40% for 2024), excluding data leakage. Across 3 runs, SDAgent-DT jointly fulfilled a core set of 796 requirements but 526 were uniquely fulfilled in only one run, suggesting best-of-N gains at high cost.
extraction.limitations: Internal validity is threatened by possible implementation errors in the unified agent framework, which could confound the architectural comparison (mitigated by code review and public release). External validity is limited to two models (Gemini-2.5-Pro and -Flash) and the authors' own benchmark, though requirements were revised by human experts. Construct validity rests on the reliability of the LLM-as-Judge requirement-fulfilment component, validated only by consistency with human expert assessments.

evidence_notes.finding: A vision paper proposing ALMAS, a tiered multi-agent framework aligning agents with agile roles across the full SDLC, in which a Supervisor Agent routes sub-tasks to cheaper or stronger LLMs by complexity and Meta-RAG code summaries mitigate context limits; the framework is demonstrated only on one illustrative application-generation use case, with end-to-end evaluation explicitly deferred.
evidence_notes.quote: Looking ahead, we plan to conduct end-to-end evaluations of ALMAS on a range of coding tasks.

extraction.agent_count: 6+ named agents (Sprint, Supervisor, Summary, Control, Developer/Code, Peer Review)
extraction.key_results: Agents map to agile roles: Sprint Agent acts as Product Manager/Scrum Master producing sub-tasks with acceptance criteria and few-shot effort estimates; Supervisor Agent routes sub-tasks across a diverse LLM pool by specialty, size and cost; Summary Agent builds structured natural-language code summaries and the Control Agent retrieves over them (Meta-RAG) to address context-window limits and attention dilution; Developer Agent checks formatting, compilation and unit tests; Peer Agent reviews for vulnerabilities, performance, hallucinations and formal verification. Failed tests trigger the Control Agent to re-localize, and after several failed recovery attempts control passes to a human with a summarized action history. Demonstration used GPT-4o for all agents with Jira and Bitbucket integration to build a Streamlit stock-options visualization app and then add a bar-chart feature. The paper positions agile role alignment, dynamic summarization and Meta-RAG as mitigations for the poor task verification and communication breakdowns reported in prior multi-agent failure analyses.
extraction.limitations: This is a vision/blueprint paper: agents were previously evaluated only in isolation, the multi-agent demonstration is a single non-quantitative use case, and the authors state the necessary end-to-end evaluation will be explored in future work using datasets such as SWE-Bench along with intermediate metrics like localization efficiency. No baseline, no comparison against single-agent operation, and no reported success rates, costs or latencies.

evidence_notes.finding: Across VerilogEvalV2 and RTLLM-v2.0, frontier models paired with a single-agent ReAct reflection loop and simulator feedback reached 89.74% and 96.08%, matching or exceeding prior multi-agent orchestration and fine-tuned RTL pipelines; the authors read this as benchmark saturation rather than as evidence that multi-agent specialization is unnecessary in general.
evidence_notes.quote: This suggests a shift in the evaluation landscape: stronger base models plus minimal iterative refinement can match more elaborate pipelines, raising the bar for benchmark design and analysis going forward.

extraction.framework: LangGraph stateful ReAct-style reflection loop with MCP-backed Icarus Verilog compilation and simulation; review covers 31 prior works including multi-agent RTL systems (MAGE, VerilogCoder, AIVRIL, AssertLLM, Autosilicon, VeriOpt)
extraction.baseline: Single-shot generation scored as pass@5; plus published results from prior domain-specific pipelines (Pinkney et al. 62.6%, Autosilicon 73.8%, VeriReason 83%/83.1%)
extraction.key_results: VerilogEval baseline -> agentic: GPT-4.1 75% -> 85.26%; GPT-4.1-mini 73.08% -> 80.77%; Claude Sonnet 4 73.72% -> 89.74% (largest gain); Llama-4-Maverick 62.82% -> 74.36%. RTLLM: GPT-4.1 88.24% -> 96.08%; Sonnet-4 90.2% -> 96.08%; Llama-4-Maverick 66.00% -> 71.43%; GPT-4.1-mini regressed from 90.2% baseline to 82.35% under agentic refinement. Agentic refinement partly offsets model-scale limits for the open-weight model. Temperature 0.7, up to 10 refinement iterations. radix2_div failed across all models and settings. Recurring failure modes: FSM mis-sequencing, handshake protocol drift, blocking vs non-blocking misuse, bit-width/borrow errors, missing finalization, sign rules, state-space oversimplification, and absent internal verification. Review classifies 31 works over eight methodological dimensions and notes agentic execution became dominant in late 2024.
extraction.limitations: The authors report partial benchmark saturation, so aggregate pass rates are no longer discriminative and mask qualitative differences in architectural reasoning. Both benchmarks emphasize single-module, short-context, repository-independent designs and rarely require hierarchical composition, so they measure localized synthesis rather than system-level reasoning. Functional testbench pass/fail is the sole primary metric, ignoring PPA, timing feasibility and maintainability. Complex handshake protocols and concurrency-heavy designs are underrepresented. Benchmark construction artifacts required prompt and testbench corrections during evaluation, making it hard to separate intrinsic model failure from dataset noise.

evidence_notes.finding: Testing 27 permutations of three local LLMs across three agent roles in the PathFinder GUI-testing multi-agent system, the hypothesis that heterogeneous specialist LLMs beat a single shared LLM was rejected per-site (homogeneous constellations won on specific websites) and only weakly supported across sites (best mixed 0.703 F1 vs 0.660 for all-Gemma2), a marginal difference.
evidence_notes.quote: We cannot accept our hypothesis H1, as one-model MALLMs tend to perform better on specifc websites.

extraction.framework: PathFinder (Multi-Agent LLM / MALLM framework for exploratory web GUI testing)
extraction.agent_count: 4 (Perceptron/summarization, System 1/decision-making, Entry Bot/data extraction, Oracle/validation); LLM varied across the first 3
extraction.key_results: 27 permutations of Mistral-Nemo, Gemma2 and Llama3.1 across 3 agent roles, on 4 e-commerce sites (demo1, demo2, ikea, netonnet), locally hosted via Ollama. H1 (mixed models beat a single model for a specific system under test) rejected; H2 (mixed models beat a single model for a generic system under test) accepted. Best cross-site F1: llama3.1/mistral-nemo/mistral-nemo 0.703 and mistral-nemo/mistral-nemo/gemma2 0.702, vs all-Gemma2 0.660 and all-Llama3.1 0.654; worst was mistral-nemo/gemma2/gemma2 at 0.306. Per-site F1 varied from 0.0 to 1.0 for the same constellation, and site complexity drove both step count (5-32 steps) and duration (2.9-72.5 minutes). A RandomForest classifier distinguished which LLM generated a scene description with >94% accuracy from length, noun-to-verb ratio and adjective count, supporting a 'mutual unintelligibility' hypothesis that models coordinate better with same-family models. A 'no prompt fits them all' effect was observed where Llama3.1 echoed the SCENE_IDENTIFICATION instruction instead of producing output, degrading downstream decisions.
extraction.limitations: The authors classify the experiment as failed with respect to H1 while still answering the research question. Only one high-level task (complete a purchase) was given, delimiting representativeness; only 4 websites and 3 comparably sized offline models were used, and generalization may not hold for substantially more powerful models such as GPT-4o. Technical threats include web scraping/parsing failures on dynamic content and JavaScript, possible Ollama model-switching and API failures disrupting agent coordination, and workflow bugs that are hard to trace given system complexity. The observed single-vs-mixed gap is described as marginal, implying model choice may matter only for optimization.
